newsitem.title: BELARUS: Key facts about Belarus referendum voting. [CORRECTED 00:05 GMT 25/11]
newsitem.headline: Key facts about Belarus referendum voting. [CORRECTED 00:05 GMT 25/11]

text.p: Here are the key facts about the referendum in the former Soviet republic of Belarus in which voting began on November 9 and ends on November 24.

ELECTORATE - Half (Corrects from two thirds) of the 7,204,000 voters aged over 18 must take part for the referendum results to be valid. Some districts have reported a turn-out as high us 50 percent in early voting. The winning constitutional draft will need the backing of 50 percent plus one registered voters.
POLLING STATIONS - There are 6,752 polling stations in the former Soviet republic's six regions -- Minsk, Brest, Grodna, Mogilyov, Vitebsk and Gomel.
OPENING TIMES - Polling stations are open at 6 a.m. (0400 GMT) and close at 10 p.m. (2000 GMT).
TURNOUT - Turnout figures will be released every four hours from 1040 a.m. (0840 GMT). Preliminary results should be available at some point on Monday, officials say.

COUNTING PROCEDURE - Local electoral commissions will count votes and pass them to the central electoral commission in the capital Minsk, which will rule on whether voting was free and fair. The commission's chief, Viktor Gonchar, who was elected by parliament, was sacked nine days ago by President Alexander Lukashenko and replaced by Lidiya Yermoshina. Gonchar had vowed not to recognise the results, saying there had been mass violations. He said Lukashenko's administration had printed voting papers and his commission had not had a chance to count them before they were distributed.
SPOILED PAPERS - Ballot papers where both Lukashenko's and parliament's draft constitutions are either supported or opposed will not be counted.

BY-ELECTIONS - Only 199 deputies were elected at the last parliamentary polls in late 1995 and by-elections for the remaining 51 seats will run parallel to the referendum vote. But the elections, and voting for some municipal authorities, have been completely overshadowed by the political battle over the referendum. There has been virtually no mention of them in state media, on which Lukashenko has a tight grip.
